item.title: Module 1: Red Team Methodology
item.description: The seven-phase red team methodology: preparation, intelligence, reconnaissance, access, post exploitation, cleanup and backout, and reporting, with the judgment behind each.
item.content:encoded: <p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Red Team Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Red Team Course</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Red team methodology</strong> connects an agreed business question to a controlled test and evidence the customer is able to use. This course uses seven phases to organize the work, with feedback between phases as observations change the plan. Your outcome is an evidence-backed conclusion, an explained limit, and a verified restoration record.</p> <p><em>Allow 25 minutes for reading and 30 minutes for the tabletop exercise. No attack tooling is required for this module.</em></p> <h2 id="learning-outcomes"> <a href="#learning-outcomes" title="Learning Outcomes">Learning Outcomes</a> <a href="#learning-outcomes" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Learning Outcomes">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Recall the phases:</strong> place a technique within a larger operation.</li> <li><strong>Explain the objective:</strong> distinguish access, business impact, and assessment evidence.</li> <li><strong>Apply a planning method:</strong> connect an approved action to a specific observation.</li> <li><strong>Evaluate a result:</strong> distinguish prevention, missing telemetry, and insufficient evidence.</li> <li><strong>Create a test plan:</strong> define entry conditions, stopping points, cleanup, and acceptance criteria.</li> </ul> <h2 id="the-seven-phases"> <a href="#the-seven-phases" title="The Seven Phases">The Seven Phases</a> <a href="#the-seven-phases" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Seven Phases">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The seven-phase model</strong> is this course’s organizing convention. It is not the MITRE ATT&CK matrix, an official maturity score, or a guarantee of one correct sequence. An operation often returns to reconnaissance after a new observation, and some tests finish without persistence or a domain-controller objective.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Phase</th> <th>Main question</th> <th>Deliverable</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Mission preparation</strong></td> <td>What is authorized and ready?</td> <td>Scope, test conditions, contacts, and infrastructure inventory</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Open-source intelligence</strong></td> <td>What does public information support?</td> <td>Attributed observations with confidence and collection dates</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Active reconnaissance</strong></td> <td>What does interaction with the approved environment reveal?</td> <td>A bounded target and dependency map</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Target exploitation</strong></td> <td>Does the selected route produce the intended test condition?</td> <td>Reproducible evidence of success, prevention, or a limit</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Post exploitation</strong></td> <td>Which approved objective follows from the obtained context?</td> <td>An access path and its observed effects</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cleanup and backout</strong></td> <td>What must be removed or restored?</td> <td>Artifact ledger, backout actions, and baseline verification</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Mission objective and reporting</strong></td> <td>What did the assessment prove?</td> <td>Findings, restoration evidence, and remediation priorities</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Cleanup, backout, and reporting begin during preparation.</strong> They are not tasks postponed until the final day. An operation lacking an artifact register, original-state record, or timestamps is difficult to explain even when the technical action succeeds.</p> <h2 id="objectives-before-techniques"> <a href="#objectives-before-techniques" title="Objectives Before Techniques">Objectives Before Techniques</a> <a href="#objectives-before-techniques" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Objectives Before Techniques">#</a> </h2> <p>A <strong>mission objective</strong> states the question the assessment is intended to answer. “Obtain administrator access” is incomplete unless it explains which business or control outcome the access tests. A customer might instead need evidence about segregation between application roles or the ability to recognize one defined behavior.</p> <p><strong>Illustrative objective:</strong> Determine whether a synthetic finance user is permitted to read a restricted sample report outside their role. The sample report contains no real financial data. Success means the test establishes an access-control result and collects enough evidence to reproduce the conclusion.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Weak objective</th> <th>More useful formulation</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Get a shell</strong></td> <td>Determine whether the approved entry route reaches the designated lab execution context</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Become domain admin</strong></td> <td>Evaluate the named privilege boundary supporting the agreed business scenario</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Avoid detection</strong></td> <td>Measure which approved behaviors produce telemetry, alerts, and analyst action</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Exfiltrate data</strong></td> <td>Demonstrate the approved data path using a designated synthetic marker and transfer limit</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>An objective also defines when to stop.</strong> If a sample-file read answers the question, copying an entire share adds data exposure without improving the finding. The test plan should identify the minimum proof before an operator reaches the resource.</p> <h2 id="use-attck-precisely"> <a href="#use-attck-precisely" title="Use ATT&CK Precisely">Use ATT&CK Precisely</a> <a href="#use-attck-precisely" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Use ATT&CK Precisely">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>MITRE ATT&CK</strong> provides a vocabulary for adversary behavior. A tactic describes an adversary goal, while a technique describes behavior supporting a goal. Map a specific observation to a technique when the evidence supports it, then retain the actual procedure and environment details alongside the mapping. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MITRE guidance on adversary emulation and red teaming"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://attack.mitre.org/resources/get-started/adversary-emulation-and-red-teaming/"> <a href="https://attack.mitre.org/resources/get-started/adversary-emulation-and-red-teaming/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >MITRE guidance on adversary emulation and red teaming</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>A technique identifier is not a test result.</strong> Listing an identifier does not establish whether an action executed, whether a sensor recorded it, or whether an analyst understood it. Different implementations of a related behavior also exercise different prerequisites and telemetry.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/objective-evidence-review-loop.webp", "caption": "Diagram linking an assessment objective to an approved test, collected evidence, and a review decision", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-22 04:18:56.232801418 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b324.887893855", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-22 04:18:56.232801418 +0000 UTC m=+324.887893855"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/objective-evidence-review-loop.webp" alt="Diagram linking an assessment objective to an approved test, collected evidence, and a review decision"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Every test needs a question, a bounded action, and evidence supporting its conclusion</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="preparation-and-scope"> <a href="#preparation-and-scope" title="Preparation and Scope">Preparation and Scope</a> <a href="#preparation-and-scope" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Preparation and Scope">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Mission preparation</strong> establishes the assets, actions, identities, and time windows included in the exercise. It also records exclusions, data-handling rules, operational contacts, and the restoration process. NIST’s assessment guidance provides a planning reference for these decisions. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="NIST SP 800-115"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/115/final"> <a href="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/115/final" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >NIST SP 800-115</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Deconfliction</strong> is the process for comparing suspicious activity with the team’s authorized actions. A matching source address alone is weak evidence. Use timestamps, action identifiers, hosts, accounts, and operator records to distinguish the exercise from an unrelated incident.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Planning item</th> <th>Example decision</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Target boundary</strong></td> <td>Only the named lab application and two test accounts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Permitted action</strong></td> <td>Attempt a read of the designated synthetic report</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Stop condition</strong></td> <td>An unrelated production record appears</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Contact</strong></td> <td>Named exercise controller and a tested backup channel</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Restoration</strong></td> <td>Remove test grants and verify the baseline role assignments</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Scope changes require a recorded decision.</strong> A newly reachable system or interesting credential is an observation, not an extension of the approved target list. Bring the observation to the exercise controller before treating it as another test step.</p> <h2 id="osint-and-active-reconnaissance"> <a href="#osint-and-active-reconnaissance" title="OSINT and Active Reconnaissance">OSINT and Active Reconnaissance</a> <a href="#osint-and-active-reconnaissance" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="OSINT and Active Reconnaissance">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Open-source intelligence (OSINT)</strong> uses publicly available information. Its collection method determines whether it touches customer-controlled infrastructure. Reading an archived page differs from browsing the customer’s live site, and public content still produces access logs when requested directly.</p> <p><strong>Active reconnaissance</strong> deliberately interacts with a target to answer a specific question. The important distinction is the collection path and the resulting evidence, not an absolute claim about generating zero alerts. Document both third-party sources and direct interactions.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Collection</th> <th>Likely observation point</th> <th>Limitation</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Third-party archive</strong></td> <td>Archive provider</td> <td>Historical content might be stale</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Public registration record</strong></td> <td>Registry or lookup provider</td> <td>Ownership does not establish test authorization</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Live customer webpage</strong></td> <td>Customer web or proxy logs</td> <td>Public access is still direct interaction</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Approved service probe</strong></td> <td>Target network and service logs</td> <td>A response establishes only the tested condition</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Reconnaissance produces hypotheses.</strong> A banner suggesting an older product version is a lead to validate, not proof of an exploitable vulnerability. A missing response likewise does not prove a host is absent.</p> <h2 id="exploitation-and-post-exploitation"> <a href="#exploitation-and-post-exploitation" title="Exploitation and Post Exploitation">Exploitation and Post Exploitation</a> <a href="#exploitation-and-post-exploitation" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Exploitation and Post Exploitation">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Target exploitation</strong> tests a selected route within the agreed conditions. Select the route because it answers the objective and fits the risk constraints. There is no requirement to demonstrate every possible weakness or to persist after every successful entry.</p> <p><strong>Post exploitation</strong> evaluates the context obtained after access. Identity, privilege, reachable resources, and dependencies determine which approved next step is meaningful. Extra persistence or lateral movement adds work and artifacts, so it needs a reason tied to the scenario.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Result</th> <th>Useful next decision</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Route prevented</strong></td> <td>Preserve prevention evidence and determine whether another route is part of scope</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Low-privilege access obtained</strong></td> <td>Record the context and test the permitted objective</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Objective already satisfied</strong></td> <td>Stop expansion and validate evidence and restoration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Unexpected sensitive access</strong></td> <td>Pause and use the agreed deconfliction channel</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A domain controller is one possible dependency</strong>, not the destination of every operation. The assessment might finish at a file-server permission boundary or a cloud application’s role check. Explain the business significance of the result instead of treating domain control as a universal score.</p> <h2 id="supplemental-video"> <a href="#supplemental-video" title="Supplemental Video">Supplemental Video</a> <a href="#supplemental-video" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Supplemental Video">#</a> </h2> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Adversary Emulation: Generating MITRE ATT&CK Technique Sequences"> <meta itemprop="description" content="YouTube Video"> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/tvQbh0bawEM/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tvQbh0bawEM"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="tvQbh0bawEM" videotitle="Adversary Emulation: Generating MITRE ATT&CK Technique Sequences" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tvQbh0bawEM" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Adversary Emulation: Generating MITRE ATT&CK Technique Sequences"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Adversary Emulation: Generating MITRE ATT\u0026CK Technique Sequences", "description": "YouTube Video", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/tvQbh0bawEM\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tvQbh0bawEM", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p><strong>Watch:</strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Adversary Emulation: Generating MITRE ATT&CK Technique Sequences"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tvQbh0bawEM"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tvQbh0bawEM" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Adversary Emulation: Generating MITRE ATT&CK Technique Sequences</a> </span> , presented by Martin Eian and published by FIRST. The presentation examines dependencies between techniques when assembling an emulation sequence. Use it to assess why a list of behaviors needs an execution plan.</p> <p><strong>Viewing task:</strong> Pick two behaviors from a fictional scenario and write the prerequisite connecting them. Then identify one condition under which the second behavior would be irrelevant. Compare the dependency with the objective instead of assuming a longer sequence is a better test.</p> <h2 id="evidence-has-several-stages"> <a href="#evidence-has-several-stages" title="Evidence Has Several Stages">Evidence Has Several Stages</a> <a href="#evidence-has-several-stages" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Evidence Has Several Stages">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Execution, collection, alerting, and response</strong> are different outcomes. A successful test action might produce an event without generating an alert. An alert might exist without reaching an analyst inside the evaluation window. Report each observed stage separately.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Stage</th> <th>Evidence needed</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Action executed</strong></td> <td>Operator record and observed target-side result</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Telemetry collected</strong></td> <td>Relevant event present at the expected sensor or collector</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Detection generated</strong></td> <td>Alert tied to the test’s entity and time</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Analyst response</strong></td> <td>Case activity showing interpretation and an action</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Restoration verified</strong></td> <td>Comparison against the agreed baseline</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>An empty search is not a detection verdict.</strong> The event might be missing because logging was disabled, collection failed, timestamps differ, or the search selected the wrong host. Resolve these possibilities before classifying a control gap.</p> <p><strong>Illustrative reasoning:</strong> A file-access exercise succeeds at 10:05 UTC. The operator has a screenshot, but the analyst searches local time and finds no event. The first follow-up is time and collection correlation, not a claim of undetected access.</p> <h2 id="cleanup-and-backout"> <a href="#cleanup-and-backout" title="Cleanup and Backout">Cleanup and Backout</a> <a href="#cleanup-and-backout" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Cleanup and Backout">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Cleanup</strong> removes artifacts owned by the exercise. <strong>Backout</strong> returns modified systems to the agreed baseline. The two actions overlap, but they are not identical. A newly created test value might be removed, while a pre-existing permission change needs its recorded original value restored.</p> <p><strong>Plan the backout before the first state change.</strong> Record the owner, original value, affected process, trigger, evidence location, and verification step. Preserve customer logs and assessment evidence according to the engagement agreement. Backout does not mean erasing the record of what happened.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Backout item</th> <th>Required evidence</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Created artifact</strong></td> <td>Ownership record, removal result, and absence check</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Modified setting</strong></td> <td>Original value, narrow restoration, and comparison</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Running process</strong></td> <td>Process owner, stop action, and later state</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Service or task</strong></td> <td>Configuration baseline, state, and trigger retest</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Customer evidence</strong></td> <td>Retention decision and report reference</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Backout completion is a finding</strong>, not an assumption. Mark each item verified, unresolved, or retained by agreement. If another administrator changed the same object, pause the reversal and use the named owner to resolve the conflict.</p> <p><strong>Exercise:</strong> Add a cleanup and backout section to the synthetic finance-report test card. List one created artifact, one modified setting, one running process, and the evidence proving each final state. State the condition preventing backout from proceeding safely.</p> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> The artifact register determines ownership. The original-state record determines restoration. A process check determines whether the removed trigger left an existing instance running. A conflict with a later administrator change requires owner review rather than an automatic overwrite.</p> <h2 id="design-one-bounded-test"> <a href="#design-one-bounded-test" title="Design One Bounded Test">Design One Bounded Test</a> <a href="#design-one-bounded-test" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Design One Bounded Test">#</a> </h2> <p>Use this <strong>test-card template</strong> before a tabletop or lab exercise:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Business question: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Approved assets and identities: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Required starting context: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Behavior and ATT&CK mapping, if justified: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Permitted action and maximum scope: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Expected operator-side evidence: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Expected defender-side observation: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Stop conditions and controller contact: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Restoration steps and verification: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Observed result, limitations, and next decision: </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Micro emulation plans</strong> provide examples of narrowly scoped tests organized around specific behaviors. Their value is repeatability and an explicit relationship between action and observation. Adapt the idea to the customer question rather than treating a public plan as approval to run it. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MITRE Center for Threat-Informed Defense project"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ctid.mitre.org/projects/micro-emulation-plans/"> <a href="https://ctid.mitre.org/projects/micro-emulation-plans/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >MITRE Center for Threat-Informed Defense project</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Exercise:</strong> Create a card for the synthetic finance-report scenario. Include an authorized reader and a restricted reader, the exact sample resource, a collection window, and the restoration check. Record what would establish a permission problem and what would leave the result inconclusive.</p> <h2 id="evaluate-your-test-card"> <a href="#evaluate-your-test-card" title="Evaluate Your Test Card">Evaluate Your Test Card</a> <a href="#evaluate-your-test-card" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Evaluate Your Test Card">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> The authorized reader establishes a baseline for the resource’s availability. The restricted reader tests the intended access boundary. A successful unauthorized read supports the access-control finding, while a timeout requires investigation before it supports any permission conclusion.</p> <p><strong>Improve the plan</strong> by adding one controlled variation. For example, repeat the same read after correcting the sample folder permission. Keep the identities, resource, and collection method stable so the comparison answers a clear question.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Review question</th> <th>A useful answer contains</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>What is being tested?</strong></td> <td>A named business or control boundary</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What changes?</strong></td> <td>One explicit action or configuration difference</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What proves the result?</strong></td> <td>Evidence from the relevant layer</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What ends the test?</strong></td> <td>A success condition, limit, or stop rule</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What remains afterward?</strong></td> <td>An artifact inventory and verified baseline</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="self-check"> <a href="#self-check" title="Self-Check">Self-Check</a> <a href="#self-check" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Self-Check">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Seven phases:</strong> Which phases repeat after new evidence appears?</li> <li><strong>OSINT:</strong> Why does publicly available information not imply zero interaction?</li> <li><strong>ATT&CK:</strong> What does a technique identifier leave unspecified?</li> <li><strong>Post exploitation:</strong> When is additional persistence unnecessary?</li> <li><strong>Negative result:</strong> What must you examine before calling an action undetected?</li> </ol> <p><strong>Answer key:</strong> Reconnaissance and planning repeat as the situation changes. Public resources still have collection paths and access logs. ATT&CK identifiers leave procedure, prerequisites, and actual test results to document.</p> <p><strong>Operation decisions:</strong> Persistence is unnecessary when the objective does not require it. An undetected-action claim needs verified execution, appropriate collection, a valid search, and a defined observation window. Cleanup and backout need their own final-state evidence.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Keep your test card</strong> and refine its infrastructure and deconfliction requirements in <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Module 2: Mission Preparation and Infrastructure"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course/mission-preparation-and-infrastructure/"> <a href="/red-team-course/mission-preparation-and-infrastructure/" rel="follow me" >Module 2: Mission Preparation and Infrastructure</a> </span> </strong>. Return to the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="course hub"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >course hub</a> </span> </strong> for the module sequence.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: CompTIA A+ (220-1201): Mobile Devices
item.category: "CompTIA A+ Course" , "Mobile Devices" , "Laptops" , "Hardware Fundamentals" , "IT Support" , "CompTIA Certification" , "Help Desk" , "Smartphones" , "Tablets" , "Computer Hardware"
item.description: Master mobile devices for the CompTIA A+ 220-1201 Core 1 exam. Learn laptop hardware, accessories and connectivity, network connectivity, MDM, and mobile synchronization.
item.content:encoded: <p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Click Here to Return To the CompTIA A+ Course Page"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus-start/"> <a href="/a-plus-start/" rel="follow me" >Click Here to Return To the CompTIA A+ Course Page</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Mobile Devices</strong> is <strong>13%</strong> of the <strong>CompTIA A+ 220-1201 Core 1</strong> exam. This module covers laptop hardware repair, accessories, connectivity, mobile device management, and synchronization. <em>Mobile support is daily work at any help desk, so know the parts and the settings cold.</em></p> <p>Laptops, smartphones, and tablets pack desktop power into sealed, compact bodies. You repair them with the right replacement parts, connect them with the right cables and radios, and manage them with policy. This module builds the hands-on knowledge you need to support users on the move.</p> <h2 id="laptop-hardware-and-components"> <a href="#laptop-hardware-and-components" title="Laptop Hardware and Components">Laptop Hardware and Components</a> <a href="#laptop-hardware-and-components" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Laptop Hardware and Components">#</a> </h2> <p>You replace failed parts inside laptops. Unlike desktops, laptop parts are small, often glued, and model-specific.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Component</th> <th>Replacement notes</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Battery</strong></td> <td>Lithium-ion, often glued in. A <em>swollen battery</em> is a fire risk and a mandatory replacement</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Keyboard</strong></td> <td>Often riveted to the chassis on thin models</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RAM</strong></td> <td>Uses <strong>SODIMM</strong> modules, smaller than desktop DIMMs</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Storage</strong></td> <td>M.2 NVMe, 2.5-inch SATA, or soldered storage</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Wireless card</strong></td> <td>Mini-PCIe or M.2 with antenna leads</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Always power down, unplug, and use an <strong>ESD strap</strong> before opening a laptop. <em>Document screw locations because they vary in length and placement.</em></p> <h2 id="display-components"> <a href="#display-components" title="Display Components">Display Components</a> <a href="#display-components" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Display Components">#</a> </h2> <p>Laptop displays combine several layers you must identify.</p> <ul> <li><strong>LCD panel types</strong> trade cost for quality: <strong>TN</strong> is cheap and fast but has poor angles, <strong>VA</strong> offers deep contrast, and <strong>IPS</strong> delivers the best color and viewing angles.</li> <li><strong>OLED</strong> lights each pixel individually for true blacks and higher contrast.</li> <li><strong>Touchscreen digitizers</strong> sit on top of the panel and convert touch into input.</li> <li><strong>Inverters</strong> powered backlights on older CCFL displays, while modern panels use <strong>LED backlights</strong>.</li> <li>A <strong>webcam and microphone</strong> live in the top bezel, with <strong>Wi-Fi antenna wires</strong> routed through the display hinges.</li> </ul> <h2 id="accessories-and-connectivity"> <a href="#accessories-and-connectivity" title="Accessories and Connectivity">Accessories and Connectivity</a> <a href="#accessories-and-connectivity" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Accessories and Connectivity">#</a> </h2> <p>You connect mobile devices with the right ports and protocols.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Connection</th> <th>Use</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>USB-C</strong></td> <td>Reversible connector for data, video, and power delivery</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Lightning</strong></td> <td>Older Apple connector for charging and data</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>NFC</strong></td> <td>Short-range tap for payments and pairing</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Bluetooth</strong></td> <td>Wireless peripherals like headsets and keyboards</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Hotspot/Tethering</strong></td> <td>Shares a phone’s cellular data with other devices</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>USB-C with Power Delivery</strong> charges laptops and phones over one cable. <em>Bluetooth pairing requires the device to be discoverable, then confirmed on both ends.</em></p> <h2 id="mobile-network-connectivity"> <a href="#mobile-network-connectivity" title="Mobile Network Connectivity">Mobile Network Connectivity</a> <a href="#mobile-network-connectivity" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Mobile Network Connectivity">#</a> </h2> <p>You configure how devices reach the internet and the carrier.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Cellular data</strong> spans <strong>3G, 4G/LTE, and 5G</strong>. Newer generations support higher peak rates, but actual service depends on coverage, spectrum, device, and congestion.</li> <li>A <strong>SIM</strong> or <strong>eSIM</strong> holds the subscriber identity that authenticates the device on the carrier network.</li> <li>A <strong>hotspot</strong> turns the device into a Wi-Fi access point for other devices.</li> <li><strong>Airplane mode</strong> changes radio settings for flights or troubleshooting. Check the device because Wi-Fi or Bluetooth might remain available or be turned back on separately.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Location services</strong> combine <strong>GPS satellites</strong> with <strong>cellular and Wi-Fi positioning</strong> for faster, indoor-capable location fixes. <em>Disabling GPS saves battery but breaks maps and find-my-device features.</em></p> <h2 id="mobile-device-management-and-synchronization"> <a href="#mobile-device-management-and-synchronization" title="Mobile Device Management and Synchronization">Mobile Device Management and Synchronization</a> <a href="#mobile-device-management-and-synchronization" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Mobile Device Management and Synchronization">#</a> </h2> <p>You manage fleets of devices with policy and keep their data in sync.</p> <p><strong>Mobile Device Management (MDM)</strong> pushes settings, apps, and security policy to corporate and <strong>BYOD</strong> (bring your own device) phones. MDM enforces passcodes, remote wipe, and encryption from a central console.</p> <p><strong>Synchronization</strong> keeps mail, calendar, and contacts consistent across devices. You sync to the cloud, to a desktop, or to an automobile.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Sync target</th> <th>Example</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Cloud</strong></td> <td>Microsoft 365, iCloud, Google</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Desktop</strong></td> <td>Local backup over USB</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Automobile</strong></td> <td>Contacts and media over Bluetooth or USB</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>Watch data caps because large syncs over cellular can cost the user money.</em></p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>Continue Core 1 with <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Networking Fundamentals"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus/networking-fundamentals-tcp-ip-wireless-protocols/"> <a href="/a-plus/networking-fundamentals-tcp-ip-wireless-protocols/" rel="follow me" >Networking Fundamentals</a> </span> and <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Hardware Components"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus/hardware-components-cpu-ram-storage-motherboards/"> <a href="/a-plus/hardware-components-cpu-ram-storage-motherboards/" rel="follow me" >Hardware Components</a> </span> . When devices fail, apply <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Hardware and Network Troubleshooting"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus/hardware-network-troubleshooting-core1/"> <a href="/a-plus/hardware-network-troubleshooting-core1/" rel="follow me" >Hardware and Network Troubleshooting</a> </span> . For a hardened mobile platform, read <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="how to install GrapheneOS"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/guides/how-to-install-graphine-os/"> <a href="/guides/how-to-install-graphine-os/" rel="follow me" >how to install GrapheneOS</a> </span> . Return to the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="CompTIA A+ Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus-start/"> <a href="/a-plus-start/" rel="follow me" >CompTIA A+ Course</a> </span> and review <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="tips for passing CompTIA exams"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/tips-and-tricks-for-passing-comptia-exams/"> <a href="/articles/tips-and-tricks-for-passing-comptia-exams/" rel="follow me" >tips for passing CompTIA exams</a> </span> .</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Module 2: Mission Preparation and Infrastructure
item.description: Everything required before an attack: scope and rules of engagement, deconfliction, hardening the attack platform, standing up redirectors, and validating the infrastructure before go.
item.content:encoded: <p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Red Team Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Red Team Course</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Mission preparation</strong> makes an assessment reproducible and controllable before the first test action. Scope, contacts, infrastructure ownership, evidence storage, and teardown belong in the same plan. This module turns the methodology test card into an operational readiness record.</p> <p><em>Allow 25 minutes for reading and 30 minutes for a preparation review. Complete Module 1 and use your own isolated lab for technical checks.</em></p> <h2 id="learning-outcomes"> <a href="#learning-outcomes" title="Learning Outcomes">Learning Outcomes</a> <a href="#learning-outcomes" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Learning Outcomes">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Define scope:</strong> name approved assets, accounts, actions, and time windows.</li> <li><strong>Explain dependencies:</strong> separate the management path, assessment traffic, and evidence storage.</li> <li><strong>Inspect readiness:</strong> verify the paths the test depends on without assuming a webpage proves everything works.</li> <li><strong>Resolve uncertainty:</strong> pause for a recorded decision when a dependency or target is ambiguous.</li> <li><strong>Create an asset register:</strong> account for ownership, expiration, collection, and removal.</li> </ul> <h2 id="scope-is-more-than-addresses"> <a href="#scope-is-more-than-addresses" title="Scope Is More Than Addresses">Scope Is More Than Addresses</a> <a href="#scope-is-more-than-addresses" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Scope Is More Than Addresses">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>An address list</strong> is only one part of scope. An approved IP might host several tenants, a public hostname might point to a shared provider, and a login might expose both permitted and excluded resources. Record the relevant identities and actions as well as network locations.</p> <p><strong>Rules of engagement (ROE)</strong> describe how the assessment is conducted. The document should connect the objective, permitted work, exclusions, contacts, and response to unexpected events. NIST provides a rules-of-engagement template and assessment-planning guidance. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="NIST SP 800-115"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/115/final"> <a href="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/115/final" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >NIST SP 800-115</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Boundary</th> <th>Example entry</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Assets</strong></td> <td>Named lab hosts and an application tenant identifier</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Identities</strong></td> <td>Two designated synthetic accounts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Actions</strong></td> <td>Approved discovery and one sample-file permission test</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Time</strong></td> <td>Explicit start, pause, and end times with a time zone</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Exclusions</strong></td> <td>Production customer data and unrelated tenants</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Limits</strong></td> <td>Maximum requests, data volume, and permitted configuration changes</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Asset ownership and authorization are separate facts.</strong> A registration record, DNS response, or customer brand on a page is insufficient to establish permission to test the underlying service. Record any required provider or tenant authorization through the agreed engagement process.</p> <h2 id="make-stop-conditions-operational"> <a href="#make-stop-conditions-operational" title="Make Stop Conditions Operational">Make Stop Conditions Operational</a> <a href="#make-stop-conditions-operational" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Make Stop Conditions Operational">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A stop condition</strong> names an observable event and an immediate response. “Be careful” is not a useful instruction. “Pause if the sample query returns a real customer record, preserve the minimal incident reference, and contact the controller” is specific enough for another operator to follow.</p> <p><strong>A restart decision</strong> also needs an owner. After a pause, document what changed, who approved resumption, and which actions remain permitted. A timed outage window expiring does not silently renew itself.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Trigger</th> <th>Immediate action</th> <th>Decision owner</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Unexpected production data</strong></td> <td>Stop collection and preserve the minimal reference</td> <td>Exercise controller</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Service health degrades</strong></td> <td>Pause the action and record timestamps</td> <td>Service owner and controller</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Unrecognized callback or host</strong></td> <td>Stop interaction pending scope verification</td> <td>Controller</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Customer reports an incident</strong></td> <td>Compare records through the deconfliction channel</td> <td>Incident lead</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Deconfliction should work during an outage.</strong> Test a backup contact path which does not depend on the same application or network under assessment. Record who is able to stop work when the primary controller is unavailable.</p> <h2 id="separate-infrastructure-roles"> <a href="#separate-infrastructure-roles" title="Separate Infrastructure Roles">Separate Infrastructure Roles</a> <a href="#separate-infrastructure-roles" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Separate Infrastructure Roles">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The operator workstation</strong> is the management endpoint. A <strong>team server</strong> coordinates the assessment platform when one is used. A <strong>redirector</strong> forwards an approved traffic path, while an <strong>evidence store</strong> retains the records required for analysis and reporting. Some labs combine roles, but their permissions and failure dependencies still differ.</p> <p><strong>A redirector is not a guarantee of anonymity.</strong> Hosting, DNS, certificates, network logs, and server administration produce records. Its placement should follow the authorized test architecture and the customer’s expected observation points.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/engagement-infrastructure-responsibilities.webp", "caption": "Diagram separating operator management, assessment infrastructure, approved target systems, and controlled evidence storage", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-22 04:18:56.240421112 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b324.895513559", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-22 04:18:56.240421112 +0000 UTC m=+324.895513559"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/engagement-infrastructure-responsibilities.webp" alt="Diagram separating operator management, assessment infrastructure, approved target systems, and controlled evidence storage"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Map ownership and allowed communication for every assessment component</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Role</th> <th>Required inventory detail</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Operator endpoint</strong></td> <td>Responsible operator, authentication, and approved management access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Assessment server</strong></td> <td>Owner, version, listeners, and retention settings</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Redirector</strong></td> <td>Domain, address, forwarding purpose, and expiration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Evidence store</strong></td> <td>Access list, encryption, retention, and deletion owner</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Target dependency</strong></td> <td>Service owner, test boundary, and restoration contact</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Choose the smallest sufficient topology.</strong> A second approved path helps only if it addresses a real dependency and has its own cleanup plan. Two hosts on one provider, account, or network still share failure conditions. Redundancy is a design decision, not a fixed required number of servers.</p> <h2 id="build-a-lab-redirector"> <a href="#build-a-lab-redirector" title="Build a Lab Redirector">Build a Lab Redirector</a> <a href="#build-a-lab-redirector" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Build a Lab Redirector">#</a> </h2> <p>Create the redirector as a <strong>small public edge VM</strong> in the customer-approved cloud account or provider account. Keep it separate from the operator workstation, assessment server, and target network. Select a region and jurisdiction approved by the engagement owner. A nearby region reduces avoidable latency, while provider reputation, data handling, and ownership matter more than a particular country.</p> <p><strong>The redirector should have one public address and one narrowly defined upstream path.</strong> Put the assessment server behind a private tunnel or an allowlisted origin address. Do not place the redirector inside the customer production network, give it a broad internal route, or reuse it as the evidence store. Those choices turn a forwarding host into an unnecessary bridge.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Placement decision</th> <th>Recommended lab choice</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Public edge</strong></td> <td>Separate low-cost VM in the approved provider account</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Origin</strong></td> <td>Assessment server on a private tunnel or fixed allowlist</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Management</strong></td> <td>Provider console or restricted admin source, separate from test traffic</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Ingress</strong></td> <td>TCP 80/443 only when the test requires them</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Egress</strong></td> <td>Origin address and approved update or monitoring services</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Expiration</strong></td> <td>Provider, address, domain, certificate, and VM teardown dates</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>For a benign HTTP exercise, install <strong>Nginx</strong> on the edge VM and proxy one named test path to a harmless origin service. The configuration below is a template for a disposable lab. Replace the example names and address with values in the connection matrix.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo apt update </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo apt install nginx </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo install -d -m <span style="color:#ae81ff">0750</span> /etc/nginx/lab </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudoedit /etc/nginx/sites-available/lab-redirector </span></span></code></pre></div><div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-nginx" data-lang="nginx"><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#66d9ef">server</span> { </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">listen</span> <span style="color:#ae81ff">80</span>; </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">server_name</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">redirector.lab.example</span>; </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">access_log</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">/var/log/nginx/lab-redirector.access.log</span>; </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">error_log</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">/var/log/nginx/lab-redirector.error.log</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">warn</span>; </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">location</span> = <span style="color:#e6db74">/healthz</span> { </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">add_header</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">Content-Type</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">text/plain</span>; </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">return</span> <span style="color:#ae81ff">200</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">"lab</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">redirector</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">ready\n"</span>; </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> } </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">location</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">/lab/</span> { </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">proxy_pass</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">http://10.30.0.10:8080</span>; </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">proxy_set_header</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">Host</span> $host; </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">proxy_set_header</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">X-Request-ID</span> $request_id; </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">proxy_set_header</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">X-Forwarded-For</span> $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> } </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>} </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Enable the single site, check the syntax, and reload only after the configuration review:</strong></p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/lab-redirector /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/lab-redirector </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo nginx -t </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo systemctl reload nginx </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The origin address <strong>must be reachable from the redirector through the approved path</strong>. An RFC 1918 address in <code>proxy_pass</code> requires a private tunnel or a routed lab network. It does not create connectivity by itself. The origin should expose only the harmless test service and accept traffic from the redirector’s fixed address.</p> <p><strong>Test each leg with a unique request identifier.</strong> First query the edge health endpoint, then request the lab path, and finally compare the edge and origin logs. Do not use a payload, credential collector, or unrestricted forward rule for this readiness test.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>curl --fail http://redirector.lab.example/healthz </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>curl --fail -H <span style="color:#e6db74">'X-Lab-Request: prep-001'</span> http://redirector.lab.example/lab/healthz </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo journalctl -u nginx --since <span style="color:#e6db74">'5 minutes ago'</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Expected result:</strong> The health endpoint returns the fixed readiness text. The second request appears in the edge access log and the origin log with the same test identifier. A successful edge response without an origin record indicates a configuration, route, or collection problem. These commands are documentation examples for an authorized lab.</p> <p><strong>For HTTPS, use a certificate whose name matches the approved test domain</strong> and record its issuer, renewal owner, and expiry. Keep certificate automation separate from the test path. Validate TLS from the same client class used by the exercise, then preserve the certificate and access-log references in the readiness register. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Nginx proxy module documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html"> <a href="https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Nginx proxy module documentation</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Backout for the redirector</strong> is part of the build. Remove the enabled site, reload Nginx, revoke or delete the test certificate, remove the DNS record, destroy the VM, and verify the provider account has no remaining address, firewall rule, snapshot, or access key. Retain the agreed logs and teardown evidence instead of deleting the assessment record.</p> <h2 id="protect-management-and-evidence"> <a href="#protect-management-and-evidence" title="Protect Management and Evidence">Protect Management and Evidence</a> <a href="#protect-management-and-evidence" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Protect Management and Evidence">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Management access</strong> should expose only the services and sources needed by the assessment team. Define inbound and outbound requirements independently. A rule permitting all traffic from a broad customer subnet is different from a narrowly scoped management rule.</p> <p><strong>Protect the records as well as the listener.</strong> Assessment data includes credentials, screenshots, transcripts, and customer configuration. Restrict access to the people who need it, keep secrets out of command histories and shared notes, and document a retention deadline. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="NIST assessment data-handling guidance"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-115.pdf"> <a href="https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-115.pdf" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >NIST assessment data-handling guidance</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Control</th> <th>Readiness question</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Authentication</strong></td> <td>Does each operator have accountable access?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Network policy</strong></td> <td>Are necessary sources, destinations, ports, and address families explicit?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Host updates</strong></td> <td>Are the selected versions and relevant maintenance decisions recorded?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Secret storage</strong></td> <td>Are operational secrets separated from general documentation?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Evidence access</strong></td> <td>Is the reviewer able to read the required records without broad administrative access?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Recovery</strong></td> <td>Is a known recovery path available before firewall or service changes?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Do not apply an incomplete firewall snippet remotely.</strong> A copied default-drop sequence often omits established connections, loopback, management recovery, IPv6, or required infrastructure traffic. Review the actual policy against a connection matrix and test it from a recoverable lab console.</p> <h2 id="inspect-listening-services"> <a href="#inspect-listening-services" title="Inspect Listening Services">Inspect Listening Services</a> <a href="#inspect-listening-services" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Inspect Listening Services">#</a> </h2> <p>On your <strong>Linux assessment server</strong>, inspect current listeners and nftables policy without changing either:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo ss -lntup </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo nft list ruleset </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>ss</code></strong> reports socket information. <strong><code>-l</code></strong> selects listeners, <strong><code>-n</code></strong> keeps numeric addresses, <strong><code>-t</code></strong> and <strong><code>-u</code></strong> include TCP and UDP, and <strong><code>-p</code></strong> requests process information. Permissions affect which process details appear. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="ss manual"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ss.8.html"> <a href="https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ss.8.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >ss manual</a> </span> </p> <p><strong><code>nft list ruleset</code></strong> displays nftables configuration. Interpret an empty output in the context of the host’s actual firewall stack and any provider firewall. A host-level ruleset alone does not describe every control on the network path. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Netfilter ruleset-management documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://wiki.nftables.org/wiki-nftables/index.php/Operations_at_ruleset_level"> <a href="https://wiki.nftables.org/wiki-nftables/index.php/Operations_at_ruleset_level" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Netfilter ruleset-management documentation</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Expected exercise result:</strong> Every listening socket has a documented purpose and owner. An unexpected listener is a finding to explain before launch, not something to terminate blindly. Compare the output with the connection matrix and preserve the timestamp.</p> <h2 id="verify-each-connection-leg"> <a href="#verify-each-connection-leg" title="Verify Each Connection Leg">Verify Each Connection Leg</a> <a href="#verify-each-connection-leg" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Verify Each Connection Leg">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A browsable HTTPS endpoint</strong> establishes only the behavior of the request you sent. It does not establish the management path, an internal forwarding rule, the intended application exchange, or evidence collection. Test the intended path in a closed range using harmless test traffic.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Leg</th> <th>Check</th> <th>Evidence</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Name resolution</strong></td> <td>Resolve the approved domain through the intended resolver</td> <td>Name, address, resolver, and time</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>TLS endpoint</strong></td> <td>Check the certificate and successful negotiation</td> <td>Hostname, validity, and observed endpoint</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Forwarded request</strong></td> <td>Send the designated harmless lab request</td> <td>Matching ingress and application records</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Management path</strong></td> <td>Authenticate through the approved operator route</td> <td>Operator identity and access log</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Evidence collection</strong></td> <td>Locate the test record in the chosen store</td> <td>Record identifier and collection time</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Correlation beats assumption.</strong> Give the harmless test request a unique lab identifier and follow it through the expected logs. If the public endpoint succeeds but the downstream record is absent, investigate forwarding or collection before treating the entire path as ready.</p> <h2 id="domains-certificates-and-mail"> <a href="#domains-certificates-and-mail" title="Domains, Certificates, and Mail">Domains, Certificates, and Mail</a> <a href="#domains-certificates-and-mail" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Domains, Certificates, and Mail">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A TLS certificate</strong> supports authentication of the endpoint named in the certificate under the client’s trust rules. It does not certify the purpose or authorization of an assessment. Domain categorization also does not guarantee a filtering product permits traffic. Verify actual policy behavior in the approved test conditions.</p> <p><strong>A mail exercise</strong> needs a separate delivery plan. Record the sending service, approved recipients, expected message handling, and reporting channel. Begin with an inert message and a synthetic destination so routing and attribution are checked before the campaign-specific work in Module 10.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Item</th> <th>What to record</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Domain</strong></td> <td>Registrant or responsible owner, purpose, and expiration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Certificate</strong></td> <td>Subject names, issuer, validity, and renewal owner</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Mail sender</strong></td> <td>Account, sending service, authentication, and permitted recipients</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Delivery test</strong></td> <td>Message identifier, expected route, and observed result</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Teardown</strong></td> <td>Required revocation, removal, and evidence of completion</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Reputation is not a substitute for measurement.</strong> A newly registered domain being blocked is a meaningful observation about the tested policy. Whether the test should continue through another route depends on the objective and a recorded controller decision.</p> <h2 id="supplemental-video"> <a href="#supplemental-video" title="Supplemental Video">Supplemental Video</a> <a href="#supplemental-video" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Supplemental Video">#</a> </h2> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Micro Emulation Plans: Making Adversary Emulation Accessible"> <meta itemprop="description" content="YouTube Video"> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/X4VuzccCDTU/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X4VuzccCDTU"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="X4VuzccCDTU" videotitle="Micro Emulation Plans: Making Adversary Emulation Accessible" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X4VuzccCDTU" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Micro Emulation Plans: Making Adversary Emulation Accessible"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Micro Emulation Plans: Making Adversary Emulation Accessible", "description": "YouTube Video", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/X4VuzccCDTU\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X4VuzccCDTU", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p><strong>Watch:</strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Micro Emulation Plans: Making Adversary Emulation Accessible"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X4VuzccCDTU"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X4VuzccCDTU" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Micro Emulation Plans: Making Adversary Emulation Accessible</a> </span> , published by SANS Offensive Operations and featured by the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MITRE Center for Threat-Informed Defense"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ctid.mitre.org/videos/micro-emulation-plans/"> <a href="https://ctid.mitre.org/videos/micro-emulation-plans/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >MITRE Center for Threat-Informed Defense</a> </span> . Use the discussion of bounded tests to identify which infrastructure a particular objective needs.</p> <p><strong>Viewing task:</strong> Choose one proposed test and list its required identities, hosts, network paths, and observations. Remove components which do not support the test. Explain the remaining dependencies and how the operator would recognize a failed prerequisite.</p> <h2 id="rehearse-deconfliction"> <a href="#rehearse-deconfliction" title="Rehearse Deconfliction">Rehearse Deconfliction</a> <a href="#rehearse-deconfliction" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Rehearse Deconfliction">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Tabletop scenario:</strong> At 14:20 UTC, the customer reports an unexpected connection from an address assigned to the exercise. Your notes contain a different destination and a test completed ten minutes earlier. The address is shared by two approved operators.</p> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> The shared source is insufficient attribution. Compare the destination, time, account, process or request identifier, and each operator’s record. Pause relevant activity while the incident lead determines whether the event belongs to the assessment. Do not label unmatched activity as yours to simplify the conversation.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Exercise and action ID: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Time, time zone, and known clock offset: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Operator and approved source: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Target asset and account context: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Intended action and expected effect: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Observed result and evidence reference: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Unexpected behavior: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Pause/resume decision and owner: </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Review the rehearsal</strong> by checking whether another operator reconstructs the sequence from the record alone. Missing timestamps or shared anonymous access make the record less useful. Correct those gaps before the launch decision.</p> <h2 id="create-the-readiness-register"> <a href="#create-the-readiness-register" title="Create the Readiness Register">Create the Readiness Register</a> <a href="#create-the-readiness-register" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Create the Readiness Register">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Build one row per asset</strong> using the template below. Include temporary domains, provider accounts, test identities, storage locations, and any persistent assessment component. An artifact absent from the register is easy to miss during teardown.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Asset identifier and purpose: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Owner and approved operator: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Address / domain / tenant / host: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Required inbound and outbound paths: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Authentication and secret location: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Evidence and retention location: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Expiration or removal deadline: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Recovery and teardown procedure: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Verification result and reviewer: </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Go/no-go exercise:</strong> Your listeners are reachable, but the backup contact has not been tested and the evidence store rejects writes. Decide whether the operational prerequisites are satisfied. Separate technical connectivity from the ability to control and document the assessment.</p> <p><strong>Expected answer:</strong> The launch criteria are incomplete. Fix the failed evidence path, test the contact path, and record the verification. A functional connection alone does not satisfy the preparation requirements.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Retain the readiness register</strong> alongside the Module 1 test card. Continue with <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Module 3: Networking and Active Directory Foundations"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course/foundations-networking-and-active-directory/"> <a href="/red-team-course/foundations-networking-and-active-directory/" rel="follow me" >Module 3: Networking and Active Directory Foundations</a> </span> </strong> to interpret the connections and identities the plan depends on. Return to the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="course hub"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >course hub</a> </span> </strong> for the complete sequence.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: CompTIA A+ (220-1201): Networking Fundamentals
item.category: "CompTIA A+ Course" , "Networking" , "TCP/IP" , "Wireless Networking" , "IT Support" , "CompTIA Certification" , "Help Desk" , "Network Hardware" , "SOHO Networks" , "IT Fundamentals"
item.description: Master networking for the CompTIA A+ 220-1201 Core 1 exam. Learn TCP and UDP ports, wireless technologies, networked host services, network hardware, SOHO configuration, and tools.
item.content:encoded: <p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Click Here to Return To the CompTIA A+ Course Page"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus-start/"> <a href="/a-plus-start/" rel="follow me" >Click Here to Return To the CompTIA A+ Course Page</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Networking</strong> is <strong>23%</strong> of the <strong>CompTIA A+ 220-1201 Core 1</strong> exam, the second-largest domain. This module covers ports and protocols, wireless standards, host services, network hardware, SOHO setup, and tools. <em>Memorize the common ports because the exam tests them directly.</em></p> <p>Every support call eventually touches the network. You diagnose connectivity by knowing which protocol runs on which port, how wireless bands differ, and what each device on the wire does. This module gives you that foundation.</p> <h2 id="common-ports-and-protocols"> <a href="#common-ports-and-protocols" title="Common Ports and Protocols">Common Ports and Protocols</a> <a href="#common-ports-and-protocols" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Common Ports and Protocols">#</a> </h2> <p>You must know these ports by number. <strong>TCP</strong> is connection-oriented and reliable, while <strong>UDP</strong> is connectionless and fast.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Port</th> <th>Protocol</th> <th>Purpose</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>20/21</td> <td><strong>FTP</strong></td> <td>File transfer</td> </tr> <tr> <td>22</td> <td><strong>SSH/SFTP</strong></td> <td>Secure remote shell</td> </tr> <tr> <td>23</td> <td><strong>Telnet</strong></td> <td>Insecure remote shell</td> </tr> <tr> <td>25</td> <td><strong>SMTP</strong></td> <td>Sending email</td> </tr> <tr> <td>53</td> <td><strong>DNS</strong></td> <td>Name resolution</td> </tr> <tr> <td>67/68</td> <td><strong>DHCP</strong></td> <td>IP address assignment</td> </tr> <tr> <td>80</td> <td><strong>HTTP</strong></td> <td>Web traffic</td> </tr> <tr> <td>110</td> <td><strong>POP3</strong></td> <td>Receiving email</td> </tr> <tr> <td>143</td> <td><strong>IMAP</strong></td> <td>Receiving email</td> </tr> <tr> <td>443</td> <td><strong>HTTPS</strong></td> <td>Encrypted web traffic</td> </tr> <tr> <td>445</td> <td><strong>SMB</strong></td> <td>File and printer sharing</td> </tr> <tr> <td>3389</td> <td><strong>RDP</strong></td> <td>Remote desktop</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>Telnet and FTP send data in clear text, so prefer SSH and HTTPS.</em></p> <h2 id="wireless-networking"> <a href="#wireless-networking" title="Wireless Networking">Wireless Networking</a> <a href="#wireless-networking" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Wireless Networking">#</a> </h2> <p>You match the band and standard to the environment.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Band</th> <th>Trait</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>2.4 GHz</strong></td> <td>Longer range, slower, more interference</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>5 GHz</strong></td> <td>Faster, shorter range, less crowded</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>6 GHz</strong></td> <td>Newest, widest channels, Wi-Fi 6E and 7</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The <strong>802.11</strong> standards advance over time: <strong>802.11n (Wi-Fi 4)</strong>, <strong>802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5)</strong>, <strong>802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6/6E)</strong>, and <strong>802.11be (Wi-Fi 7)</strong>. Short-range radios include <strong>NFC</strong> for tap actions and <strong>RFID</strong> for tags and badges.</p> <p><em>On 2.4 GHz, use non-overlapping channels 1, 6, and 11 to avoid interference.</em></p> <h2 id="services-provided-by-networked-hosts"> <a href="#services-provided-by-networked-hosts" title="Services Provided by Networked Hosts">Services Provided by Networked
