Hosts</a> <a href="#services-provided-by-networked-hosts" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Services Provided by Networked Hosts">#</a> </h2> <p>You identify what each server role does on the network.</p> <ul> <li><strong>DNS</strong> resolves names to IP addresses.</li> <li><strong>DHCP</strong> hands out IP addresses, gateways, and DNS servers automatically.</li> <li><strong>File servers</strong> store shared documents centrally.</li> <li><strong>Print servers</strong> queue jobs to shared printers.</li> <li><strong>Proxy servers</strong> filter and cache web requests.</li> <li><strong>Web servers</strong> host sites and applications.</li> </ul> <p>You configure <strong>DNS records</strong> so services resolve correctly:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Record</th> <th>Maps</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>A</strong></td> <td>Name to IPv4 address</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>AAAA</strong></td> <td>Name to IPv6 address</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>CNAME</strong></td> <td>Name to another name (alias)</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>MX</strong></td> <td>Domain to mail server</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>TXT</strong></td> <td>Text for SPF, DKIM, verification</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="networking-hardware"> <a href="#networking-hardware" title="Networking Hardware">Networking Hardware</a> <a href="#networking-hardware" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Networking Hardware">#</a> </h2> <p>You connect and route traffic with the right device.</p> <ul> <li>A <strong>switch</strong> forwards frames between devices on the same LAN by MAC address.</li> <li>A <strong>router</strong> moves packets between networks and to the internet.</li> <li>An <strong>access point (AP)</strong> bridges wireless clients onto the wired network.</li> <li>A <strong>firewall</strong> filters traffic by rules at the boundary.</li> <li><strong>Power over Ethernet (PoE)</strong> delivers power and data over one cable to APs, cameras, and phones.</li> </ul> <h2 id="soho-network-configuration"> <a href="#soho-network-configuration" title="SOHO Network Configuration">SOHO Network Configuration</a> <a href="#soho-network-configuration" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="SOHO Network Configuration">#</a> </h2> <p>You set up small office and home networks with correct addressing.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Address type</th> <th>Use</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Static</strong></td> <td>Manually set, for servers and printers</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Dynamic (DHCP)</strong></td> <td>Auto-assigned, for clients</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>APIPA</strong></td> <td>169.254.x.x self-assigned when DHCP fails</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>IPv6</strong></td> <td>128-bit addresses for modern networks</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>A <strong>private IP range</strong> such as 192.168.0.0/16 stays inside the LAN, while <strong>NAT</strong> translates it to one public address for internet access.</p> <h2 id="networking-tools"> <a href="#networking-tools" title="Networking Tools">Networking Tools</a> <a href="#networking-tools" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Networking Tools">#</a> </h2> <p>You build and test cabling with the right tools.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Tool</th> <th>Job</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Crimper</strong></td> <td>Attaches RJ45 connectors to cable</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cable tester</strong></td> <td>Verifies wiring continuity and order</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Toner probe</strong></td> <td>Traces a cable in a bundle</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Punchdown tool</strong></td> <td>Seats wires into patch panels and jacks</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Wi-Fi analyzer</strong></td> <td>Maps signal strength and channel use</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Loopback plug</strong></td> <td>Tests a network port</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>Continue Core 1 with <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Hardware Components"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus/hardware-components-cpu-ram-storage-motherboards/"> <a href="/a-plus/hardware-components-cpu-ram-storage-motherboards/" rel="follow me" >Hardware Components</a> </span> and <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Virtualization and Cloud Computing"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus/virtualization-cloud-computing-concepts/"> <a href="/a-plus/virtualization-cloud-computing-concepts/" rel="follow me" >Virtualization and Cloud Computing</a> </span> . Diagnose connectivity in <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Hardware and Network Troubleshooting"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus/hardware-network-troubleshooting-core1/"> <a href="/a-plus/hardware-network-troubleshooting-core1/" rel="follow me" >Hardware and Network Troubleshooting</a> </span> . For home wireless design, see <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="the best Wi-Fi mesh system for consumers"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/best-wifi-mesh-system-for-consumers/"> <a href="/articles/best-wifi-mesh-system-for-consumers/" rel="follow me" >the best Wi-Fi mesh system for consumers</a> </span> and <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Ubiquiti UniFi vs TP-Link Omada"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/ubiquiti-unifi-vs-tp-link-omada/"> <a href="/articles/ubiquiti-unifi-vs-tp-link-omada/" rel="follow me" >Ubiquiti UniFi vs TP-Link Omada</a> </span> . item.title: Module 3: Networking and Active Directory Foundations
item.description: The networking and Active Directory concepts every red team technique builds on: HTTP and HTTPS, TCP and UDP, the domain controller, users, groups, and group nesting.
item.content:encoded: <p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Red Team Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Red Team Course</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Network reachability, authentication, and authorization</strong> answer different questions. A reachable server does not prove an account is valid, and a successful login does not grant every permission. This module connects web transports, directory services, DNS, and group membership so you diagnose the right layer before choosing a tool.</p> <p><em>Allow 25 minutes for reading and 20 minutes for a small domain-lab exercise. You need basic IP addressing and access to your own Windows lab.</em></p> <h2 id="learning-outcomes"> <a href="#learning-outcomes" title="Learning Outcomes">Learning Outcomes</a> <a href="#learning-outcomes" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Learning Outcomes">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Distinguish layers:</strong> separate an application protocol from its transport and encryption.</li> <li><strong>Explain the domain:</strong> identify the roles of DNS, a domain controller, and a resource server.</li> <li><strong>Trace permissions:</strong> follow a group-membership path to an explicit resource permission.</li> <li><strong>Interpret failure:</strong> distinguish name resolution, connection, authentication, and access denial.</li> <li><strong>Create an evidence map:</strong> connect observations without assuming a complete attack path.</li> </ul> <h2 id="protocols-have-different-jobs"> <a href="#protocols-have-different-jobs" title="Protocols Have Different Jobs">Protocols Have Different Jobs</a> <a href="#protocols-have-different-jobs" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Protocols Have Different Jobs">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>TCP</strong> provides an ordered byte stream with mechanisms for acknowledging and retransmitting data. <strong>UDP</strong> sends datagrams without TCP’s connection and delivery mechanisms. An application using UDP still implements additional reliability or security when its protocol requires it. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="TCP specification, RFC 9293"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html"> <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >TCP specification, RFC 9293</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Layer</th> <th>Example</th> <th>Question it answers</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Naming</strong></td> <td>DNS</td> <td>Which address or service location corresponds to this name?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Transport</strong></td> <td>TCP or UDP</td> <td>How are bytes or datagrams carried?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Channel protection</strong></td> <td>TLS</td> <td>How is the connection authenticated and protected?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Application</strong></td> <td>HTTP, SMB, LDAP</td> <td>What operation does the client request?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A port number is a clue</strong>, not proof of the application behind it. A TCP listener on port 443 still needs protocol validation. A service moved to another port keeps its application behavior, and a proxy often presents a different network endpoint from the underlying application.</p> <h2 id="http-tls-and-visibility"> <a href="#http-tls-and-visibility" title="HTTP, TLS, and Visibility">HTTP, TLS, and Visibility</a> <a href="#http-tls-and-visibility" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="HTTP, TLS, and Visibility">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>HTTPS</strong> protects HTTP traffic using a secure channel. TLS provides confidentiality and integrity for application data and supports authentication of the communicating endpoints. The protection applies between the endpoints of the TLS connection, including an inspecting proxy when one terminates the connection. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="TLS 1.3 specification, RFC 8446"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446.html"> <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >TLS 1.3 specification, RFC 8446</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Encryption does not establish ordinary behavior.</strong> A network observer still has connection-level information such as destination addresses, timing, and traffic volume. Endpoint tools and a configured inspection proxy have different visibility. A rarely used destination or an unusual initiating process remains relevant even when the content is encrypted.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Observation</th> <th>Reasonable conclusion</th> <th>Unsupported conclusion</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>TLS negotiation succeeds</strong></td> <td>The tested TLS connection was established</td> <td>The application is trustworthy</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>TCP port 443 is reachable</strong></td> <td>Something accepts connections there</td> <td>All application requests will succeed</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>HTTP body contains binary data</strong></td> <td>The application transfers binary content</td> <td>The transfer is malicious because it is not readable text</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>No plaintext in a capture</strong></td> <td>The capture lacks clear application content</td> <td>Defenders have no other evidence</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>HTTP is not limited to text pages.</strong> Images, compressed bodies, software downloads, and application data are ordinary uses of HTTP. A claim about command-and-control traffic needs evidence from the application, endpoint, or traffic pattern, rather than a blanket assumption about binary data.</p> <p><strong>HTTP/3</strong> also corrects the shortcut “web traffic always uses TCP.” It maps HTTP semantics onto QUIC, which uses UDP. Distinguish the application protocol from its transport before interpreting a capture or proposing a firewall rule. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="HTTP/3 specification, RFC 9114"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114.html"> <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >HTTP/3 specification, RFC 9114</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="read-a-tcp-exchange"> <a href="#read-a-tcp-exchange" title="Read a TCP Exchange">Read a TCP Exchange</a> <a href="#read-a-tcp-exchange" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Read a TCP Exchange">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Client Server </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>SYN ---------------------> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <--------------------- SYN-ACK </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ACK ---------------------> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Application data --------> </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>The three-way handshake</strong> establishes a TCP connection. It does not prove authentication to the application or permission to read its data. A connection failure belongs to a different diagnostic stage from a valid application response denying access.</p> <p><strong>A burst of connection attempts</strong> deserves interpretation in context. Destination count, port distribution, time interval, and the initiating application help distinguish a scan from an expected inventory job. Completing the handshake does not make scanning invisible, and a SYN scan is not inherently undetectable either.</p> <h2 id="what-active-directory-stores"> <a href="#what-active-directory-stores" title="What Active Directory Stores">What Active Directory Stores</a> <a href="#what-active-directory-stores" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Active Directory Stores">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)</strong> stores directory objects and supports identity, authentication, and administration for a domain environment. A <strong>domain controller (DC)</strong> runs those services and participates in directory replication. A deployment normally includes multiple domain controllers rather than a single universal database server. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft AD DS overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/get-started/virtual-dc/active-directory-domain-services-overview"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/get-started/virtual-dc/active-directory-domain-services-overview" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft AD DS overview</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>A domain is not a subnet.</strong> Systems in different routed networks belong to the same domain, while systems sharing a subnet belong to different domains or no domain. Separate logical identity structure from packet-routing structure in your notes.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Object or role</th> <th>Purpose</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>User account</strong></td> <td>Represents a person or application identity</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Computer account</strong></td> <td>Represents a domain-joined machine identity</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Security group</strong></td> <td>Collects principals for rights or permissions</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Organizational unit</strong></td> <td>Organizes objects for delegation and policy application</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Domain controller</strong></td> <td>Provides directory and authentication services</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Resource server</strong></td> <td>Hosts the share, application, or other resource being accessed</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Domain-controller access is not every engagement’s objective.</strong> An assessment might instead test access to one application role, a file share, or an approved synthetic record. Domain controllers are sensitive dependencies, and local workstation account secrets are not simply copies of the domain account database.</p> <h2 id="dns-finds-domain-services"> <a href="#dns-finds-domain-services" title="DNS Finds Domain Services">DNS Finds Domain Services</a> <a href="#dns-finds-domain-services" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="DNS Finds Domain Services">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>DNS service records</strong> help clients locate domain controllers and domain services. A directory operation depends on more than reaching an IP address. The client also needs appropriate naming, routing, time, authentication, and permission for the requested action. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft domain-controller location process"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/dc-locator"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/dc-locator" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft domain-controller location process</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Worked failure:</strong> A workstation reaches a file server’s address but cannot resolve the domain’s service records through its configured resolver. This supports investigating DNS configuration before calling the account invalid. Record the resolver and query result, then compare them with the intended lab configuration.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/domain-access-dependency-map.webp", "caption": "Diagram connecting DNS service location, domain authentication, resource authorization, and evidence from each stage", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-22 04:18:56.247495303 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b324.902587740", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-22 04:18:56.247495303 +0000 UTC m=+324.902587740"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/domain-access-dependency-map.webp" alt="Diagram connecting DNS service location, domain authentication, resource authorization, and evidence from each stage"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Reachability, authentication, and permission require separate evidence</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="groups-and-effective-access"> <a href="#groups-and-effective-access" title="Groups and Effective Access">Groups and Effective Access</a> <a href="#groups-and-effective-access" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Groups and Effective Access">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Security groups</strong> support permission assignments to collections of accounts and other groups. Distribution groups serve a different purpose and are not security principals for permission assignment. Group scope constrains valid membership and where permissions apply. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft security-group documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/understand-security-groups"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/understand-security-groups" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft security-group documentation</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Group names are not permission evidence.</strong> A group called Finance Admins needs an actual rights assignment or resource permission before the name establishes anything useful. A direct account entry in an access-control list is also possible. The common administrative preference for groups does not prohibit permissions assigned to an individual account.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Illustrative lab access path: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>LAB\Alice </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> member of Finance-Readers </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> member of Reports-Read </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> explicit read permission on a sample report folder </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>The membership path is only part of the decision.</strong> Inspect the intended operation, the resource’s access-control entries, and the token used for the attempt. File access through a share involves both share and filesystem permissions. Membership changes also need an appropriate session or token refresh before testing their effect.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Evidence</th> <th>What it contributes</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Directory membership</strong></td> <td>A relationship between an account and group</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Current access token</strong></td> <td>Group information available to the running process</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Resource permissions</strong></td> <td>Rights granted or denied on the target object</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Observed operation</strong></td> <td>The result for the exact action and context tested</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Illustrative decision:</strong> Alice belongs to Reports-Read and successfully reads a sample file. This proves the read operation under the tested context. It does not prove write access, local administrator rights, or access to another share with a similar name.</p> <h2 id="supplemental-video"> <a href="#supplemental-video" title="Supplemental Video">Supplemental Video</a> <a href="#supplemental-video" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Supplemental Video">#</a> </h2> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Active Directory Domain Service Deep Dive"> <meta itemprop="description" content="YouTube Video"> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/4qC7H-y7oKI/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4qC7H-y7oKI"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="4qC7H-y7oKI" videotitle="Active Directory Domain Service Deep Dive" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4qC7H-y7oKI" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Active Directory Domain Service Deep Dive"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Active Directory Domain Service Deep Dive", "description": "YouTube Video", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/4qC7H-y7oKI\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4qC7H-y7oKI", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p><strong>Watch:</strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Active Directory Domain Service Deep Dive"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4qC7H-y7oKI"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4qC7H-y7oKI" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Active Directory Domain Service Deep Dive</a> </span> , by John Savill’s Technical Training. Use the architecture explanation to connect domains, forests, and domain controllers. Record the logical relationship between the components before studying the later technique-specific modules.</p> <p><strong>Viewing task:</strong> Draw two domain controllers in one domain and two member servers on different subnets. Explain which relationship is directory membership and which relationship is network reachability. Your diagram should work without treating a subnet as a domain boundary.</p> <h2 id="observe-a-lab-connection"> <a href="#observe-a-lab-connection" title="Observe a Lab Connection">Observe a Lab Connection</a> <a href="#observe-a-lab-connection" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Observe a Lab Connection">#</a> </h2> <p>Use <strong>PowerShell</strong> on your domain-joined lab workstation. Replace the example names with your own approved domain and server:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-powershell" data-lang="powershell"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Resolve-DnsName -Name _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.lab.example -Type SRV </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Test-NetConnection -ComputerName files.lab.example -Port <span style="color:#ae81ff">445</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>whoami /groups </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>Resolve-DnsName</code></strong> asks for the specified DNS record type. <strong><code>Test-NetConnection</code></strong> tests the selected TCP destination and reports connection information. <strong><code>whoami /groups</code></strong> shows group information in your current context. None of these commands proves permission to a particular file. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Resolve-DnsName reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/dnsclient/resolve-dnsname?view=windowsserver2025-ps"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/dnsclient/resolve-dnsname?view=windowsserver2025-ps" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Resolve-DnsName reference</a> </span> , <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Test-NetConnection reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/nettcpip/test-netconnection"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/nettcpip/test-netconnection" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Test-NetConnection reference</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Record actual results.</strong> A successful TCP test indicates reachability for this connection attempt, while an unsuccessful one has several possible causes. Name resolution, routing, firewall policy, and a stopped service belong in the differential diagnosis. Do not label every failure “bad credentials.”</p> <h2 id="work-through-a-failure"> <a href="#work-through-a-failure" title="Work Through a Failure">Work Through a Failure</a> <a href="#work-through-a-failure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Work Through a Failure">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Scenario:</strong> A lab user resolves the file server, connects to port 445, and receives access denied when opening a sample report. Another approved lab user reads the same file successfully. No network or account changes have yet been made.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Check</th> <th>Observation</th> <th>Next inference</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Name resolution</strong></td> <td>Both users resolve the same server</td> <td>Compare the remaining layers</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Transport</strong></td> <td>Both connect to TCP 445</td> <td>A basic connection is available</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Identity</strong></td> <td>The users present different accounts</td> <td>Confirm which token and authentication were used</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Resource operation</strong></td> <td>One read succeeds and one fails</td> <td>Compare the exact permissions and context</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> The successful second read makes a universal service outage less likely. By itself, it does not identify the missing permission or establish whether the denied operation failed authentication or authorization. Inspect the resource and correlated records before recommending a change.</p> <p><strong>Create a dependency record</strong> for this scenario or your own lab observation. Include resolver, destination, protocol, account authority, requested operation, result, and the next evidence needed. This record becomes the starting point for the Windows identity module.</p> <h2 id="self-check"> <a href="#self-check" title="Self-Check">Self-Check</a> <a href="#self-check" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Self-Check">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>HTTPS:</strong> Which observations remain available outside the encrypted content?</li> <li><strong>HTTP/3:</strong> Why is “all web traffic uses TCP” inaccurate?</li> <li><strong>Directory structure:</strong> Does one subnet imply one domain?</li> <li><strong>Group nesting:</strong> What additional evidence turns a membership chain into a supported access claim?</li> <li><strong>Connection success:</strong> What has a successful TCP 445 test left untested?</li> </ol> <p><strong>Answer key:</strong> Addresses, timing, and volume remain useful, and endpoint or proxy visibility differs from a passive capture. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. A domain and a subnet describe different structures.</p> <p><strong>Access checks:</strong> A membership chain needs the relevant token, permissions, and requested operation. TCP reachability leaves application authentication and authorization unproven.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Keep the dependency map</strong> beside your lab notes. It helps separate a naming problem from a credential or permission problem. Continue with <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Module 4: Windows Internals and Authentication"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course/foundations-windows-internals-and-authentication/"> <a href="/red-team-course/foundations-windows-internals-and-authentication/" rel="follow me" >Module 4: Windows Internals and Authentication</a> </span> </strong>, or return to the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="course hub"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >course hub</a> </span> </strong>.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: CompTIA A+ (220-1201): Hardware Components
item.category: "CompTIA A+ Course" , "Computer Hardware" , "Motherboards" , "CPU" , "Storage" , "IT Support" , "CompTIA Certification" , "Help Desk" , "Hardware Fundamentals" , "PC Building"
item.description: Master hardware for the CompTIA A+ 220-1201 Core 1 exam. Learn cables and connectors, RAM, storage devices, motherboards and CPUs, power supplies, and printers.
item.content:encoded: <p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Click Here to Return To the CompTIA A+ Course Page"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus-start/"> <a href="/a-plus-start/" rel="follow me" >Click Here to Return To the CompTIA A+ Course Page</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Hardware</strong> is <strong>25%</strong> of the <strong>CompTIA A+ 220-1201 Core 1</strong> exam, the largest Core 1 domain. This module covers cables, RAM, storage, motherboards, CPUs, power supplies, and printers. <em>This domain is the hands-on heart of A+, so learn the parts by sight and by spec.</em></p> <p>Hardware is the physical foundation of every system you support. You pick the right RAM, install the correct drive, seat a CPU without bending pins, and size a power supply that will not fail under load. This module covers the components you touch every day.</p> <h2 id="cables-and-connectors"> <a href="#cables-and-connectors" title="Cables and Connectors">Cables and Connectors</a> <a href="#cables-and-connectors" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Cables and Connectors">#</a> </h2> <p>You match each cable to its job.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Cable</th> <th>Use</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Cat 5e/6/6a</strong></td> <td>Copper Ethernet, RJ45 connector</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fiber (single-mode)</strong></td> <td>Long distance, SC/LC connectors</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fiber (multimode)</strong></td> <td>Short distance, higher bandwidth</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>USB-C</strong></td> <td>Reversible data, power, and video</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SATA</strong></td> <td>Internal drive data</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>HDMI/DisplayPort</strong></td> <td>Digital video and audio</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Single-mode fiber</strong> carries one light path over long distances. <strong>Multimode fiber</strong> carries many paths over short runs inside a building.</p> <h2 id="ram-characteristics"> <a href="#ram-characteristics" title="RAM Characteristics">RAM Characteristics</a> <a href="#ram-characteristics" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="RAM Characteristics">#</a> </h2> <p>You install the right memory for the board and workload.</p> <ul> <li><strong>DIMM</strong> modules go in desktops, <strong>SODIMM</strong> modules go in laptops.</li> <li><strong>DDR generations</strong> are not interchangeable: <strong>DDR3, DDR4, and DDR5</strong> use different notches and voltages.</li> <li><strong>ECC</strong> (Error-Correcting Code) RAM detects and fixes memory errors in servers, while desktops use <strong>non-ECC</strong>.</li> <li><strong>Channel configuration</strong> (single, dual, quad) boosts bandwidth when you populate matched slots.</li> </ul> <p><em>Install matched pairs in the correct colored slots to enable dual-channel mode.</em></p> <h2 id="storage-devices"> <a href="#storage-devices" title="Storage Devices">Storage Devices</a> <a href="#storage-devices" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Storage Devices">#</a> </h2> <p>You choose storage by speed, interface, and form factor.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Drive</th> <th>Interface</th> <th>Speed</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>HDD</strong></td> <td>SATA</td> <td>Slowest, mechanical</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SATA SSD</strong></td> <td>SATA</td> <td>Faster, no moving parts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>NVMe SSD</strong></td> <td>PCIe (M.2)</td> <td>Fastest</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>RAID</strong> combines drives for speed or redundancy:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Level</th> <th>Behavior</th> <th>Minimum drives</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>RAID 0</strong></td> <td>Striping, speed, no redundancy</td> <td>2</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RAID 1</strong></td> <td>Mirroring, full redundancy</td> <td>2</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RAID 5</strong></td> <td>Striping with parity</td> <td>3</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RAID 6</strong></td> <td>Double parity</td> <td>4</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RAID 10</strong></td> <td>Mirror plus stripe</td> <td>4</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>RAID is not a backup. It protects against drive failure, not against deletion or ransomware.</em></p> <h2 id="motherboards-cpus-and-add-on-cards"> <a href="#motherboards-cpus-and-add-on-cards" title="Motherboards, CPUs, and Add-on Cards">Motherboards, CPUs, and Add-on Cards</a> <a href="#motherboards-cpus-and-add-on-cards" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Motherboards, CPUs, and Add-on Cards">#</a> </h2> <p>You install the core components and configure firmware.</p> <p><strong>Form factors</strong> set board size: <strong>ATX</strong> is full-size, <strong>microATX</strong> is smaller, and <strong>Mini-ITX</strong> is the smallest. <strong>CPU architecture</strong> spans <strong>x86/x64</strong> for desktops and servers and <strong>ARM</strong> for phones, tablets, and modern laptops.</p> <p>You set firmware in <strong>BIOS/UEFI</strong>: boot order, virtualization support, <strong>Secure Boot</strong>, and a <strong>TPM</strong> for encryption keys. UEFI supports modern boot features, including Secure Boot, but does not require a graphical interface or mouse. Booting from a volume larger than 2 TB also depends on partition layout, firmware, operating system, and device support.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Common UEFI settings to know: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>- Boot order / boot priority </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>- Secure Boot (on/off) </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>- TPM / fTPM enable </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>- Intel VT-x / AMD-V virtualization </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>- XMP/EXPO memory profile </span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="power-supplies"> <a href="#power-supplies" title="Power Supplies">Power Supplies</a> <a href="#power-supplies" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Power Supplies">#</a> </h2> <p>You size the <strong>power supply unit (PSU)</strong> to the system load with headroom. You match input voltage (110V/230V), wattage, and connector types (24-pin ATX, 8-pin CPU, PCIe for GPUs). <em>An undersized PSU causes random shutdowns under load.</em></p> <h2 id="printers"> <a href="#printers" title="Printers">Printers</a> <a href="#printers" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Printers">#</a> </h2> <p>You deploy and maintain multiple printer types.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Type</th> <th>How it prints</th> <th>Maintenance</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Laser</strong></td> <td>Toner fused by heat</td> <td>Replace toner, maintenance kit</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Inkjet</strong></td> <td>Sprayed liquid ink</td> <td>Clean heads, replace cartridges</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Thermal</strong></td> <td>Heat on special paper</td> <td>Replace paper, clean heating element</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Impact</strong></td> <td>Pins strike a ribbon</td> <td>Replace ribbon, used for carbon copies</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The <strong>laser imaging process</strong> has seven steps: processing, charging, exposing, developing, transferring, fusing, and cleaning. You configure drivers, network connectivity, and secure features like <strong>PIN-released printing</strong>.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>Continue Core 1 with <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Virtualization and Cloud Computing"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus/virtualization-cloud-computing-concepts/"> <a href="/a-plus/virtualization-cloud-computing-concepts/" rel="follow me" >Virtualization and Cloud Computing</a> </span> and diagnose failures in <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Hardware and Network Troubleshooting"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus/hardware-network-troubleshooting-core1/"> <a href="/a-plus/hardware-network-troubleshooting-core1/" rel="follow me" >Hardware and Network Troubleshooting</a> </span> . Review <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Networking Fundamentals"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus/networking-fundamentals-tcp-ip-wireless-protocols/"> <a href="/a-plus/networking-fundamentals-tcp-ip-wireless-protocols/" rel="follow me" >Networking Fundamentals</a> </span> for cabling context. Return to the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="CompTIA A+ Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus-start/"> <a href="/a-plus-start/" rel="follow me" >CompTIA A+ Course</a> </span> and review <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="tips for passing CompTIA exams"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/tips-and-tricks-for-passing-comptia-exams/"> <a href="/articles/tips-and-tricks-for-passing-comptia-exams/" rel="follow me" >tips for passing CompTIA exams</a> </span> .</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Module 4: Windows Internals and Authentication
item.description: How Windows stores configuration and credentials: the registry and hives, registry paths, NTLM hashes, and the difference between domain and local authentication.
item.content:encoded: <p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Red Team Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Red Team Course</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Windows security context</strong> determines which account a process represents, which objects it is permitted to access, and which user profile it reads. This module connects registry paths, security identifiers, access tokens, and authentication. You will inspect a disposable Windows VM and produce an identity record before changing anything.</p> <p><em>Allow 25 minutes for reading and 20 minutes for the optional lab. Complete the networking and Active Directory module first.</em></p> <h2 id="learning-outcomes"> <a href="#learning-outcomes" title="Learning Outcomes">Learning Outcomes</a> <a href="#learning-outcomes" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Learning Outcomes">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Identify registry context:</strong> distinguish predefined keys from the loaded hives behind them.</li> <li><strong>Read a token:</strong> separate account identity, group membership, and enabled privileges.</li> <li><strong>Explain authentication artifacts:</strong> distinguish an NT password hash from a network challenge response and a Kerberos ticket.</li> <li><strong>Check an observation:</strong> use account authority, SID, process context, and timestamps together.</li> <li><strong>Create a context record:</strong> document the identity and registry view behind each lab observation.</li> </ul> <h2 id="the-registry-model"> <a href="#the-registry-model" title="The Registry Model">The Registry Model</a> <a href="#the-registry-model" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Registry Model">#</a> </h2> <p>The <strong>registry</strong> organizes operating-system and application configuration into keys and named values. A key contains subkeys and values, while each value has a name, a type, and data. A path identifies a location, but the process context and registry view determine what a particular program reads.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> <th>Example</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Key</strong></td> <td>Container for subkeys and values</td> <td><code>Software\ExampleApp</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Value name</strong></td> <td>Identifier within a key</td> <td><code>DisplayMode</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Value type</strong></td> <td>Interpretation of the data</td> <td><code>REG_SZ</code> for a string</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Value data</strong></td> <td>Stored setting</td> <td><code>Light</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Hive</strong></td> <td>Logical registry collection with backing files</td> <td>A loaded user profile hive</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>A <strong>hive</strong> is more specific than a top-level name displayed in Registry Editor. For example, <strong><code>HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE</code></strong>, abbreviated <strong><code>HKLM</code></strong>, groups several machine hives. A user’s <strong><code>NTUSER.DAT</code></strong> backs much of their user configuration. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft registry-hive documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sysinfo/registry-hives"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sysinfo/registry-hives" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft registry-hive documentation</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="predefined-keys-and-profiles"> <a href="#predefined-keys-and-profiles" title="Predefined Keys and Profiles">Predefined Keys and Profiles</a> <a href="#predefined-keys-and-profiles" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Predefined Keys and Profiles">#</a> </h2> <p><strong><code>HKEY_USERS</code></strong>, abbreviated <strong><code>HKU</code></strong>, exposes loaded user hives. It is not an inventory of every account ever used on the machine. An existing profile on disk and a currently loaded hive are different observations.</p> <p><strong><code>HKEY_CURRENT_USER</code></strong>, abbreviated <strong><code>HKCU</code></strong>, resolves through the calling process’s user context. Do not equate it with the person sitting at the keyboard. Microsoft also documents limitations around cached predefined handles and impersonation, so programs impersonating a client need the appropriate user-key API. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft predefined-key documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sysinfo/predefined-keys"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sysinfo/predefined-keys" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft predefined-key documentation</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Calling context</th> <th>Important question</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Alice’s ordinary application</strong></td> <td>Which Alice account and SID launched this process?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Application elevated as Alice</strong></td> <td>Did elevation change privileges while retaining Alice’s identity?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Application started as Bob</strong></td> <td>Is the application reading Bob’s profile instead?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>LocalSystem service</strong></td> <td>Is the code using its service context or explicitly opening another user’s loaded hive?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Worked example:</strong> Alice’s startup entry is present in her profile. A LocalSystem service reads its own <strong><code>HKCU</code></strong> location and finds no matching value. This establishes a context mismatch, not successful removal of Alice’s entry. Record Alice’s SID and verify her specific loaded hive before drawing a conclusion.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/identity-token-registry-context.webp", "caption": "Diagram separating Windows account identity, process access token, registry profile context, and resource authorization", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-22 04:18:56.253459317 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b324.908551754", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-22 04:18:56.253459317 +0000 UTC m=+324.908551754"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/identity-token-registry-context.webp" alt="Diagram separating Windows account identity, process access token, registry profile context, and resource authorization"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>The same desktop session contains processes with different identities and privileges</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="sids-identify-principals"> <a href="#sids-identify-principals" title="SIDs Identify Principals">SIDs Identify Principals</a> <a href="#sids-identify-principals" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="SIDs Identify Principals">#</a> </h2> <p>A <strong>security identifier (SID)</strong> identifies an account or group. A display name is a label, while the SID is the identifier Windows uses in access-control decisions. Deleting and recreating an account with the same name produces a different identity. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft security-identifier documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/understand-security-identifiers"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/understand-security-identifiers" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft security-identifier documentation</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Local and domain accounts</strong> require an authority as well as a name. <strong><code>LABPC\Alice</code></strong> and <strong><code>LAB\Alice</code></strong> represent different accounts even if their display names match. Do not infer account origin from the apparent length of its SID. Local and domain account SIDs use comparable structures.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>LAB\Alice Domain account, down-level name </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>LABPC\Alice Local account on LABPC </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Alice@lab.example User principal name, when configured </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>User principal name (UPN)</strong> suffixes are configured identity names and need not match a workstation’s DNS suffix. A nonexistent prefix does not universally trigger local authentication. The logon interface, authentication provider, and requested account determine the result, including failure. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft user-name formats"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthn/user-name-formats"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthn/user-name-formats" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft user-name formats</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="processes-and-access-tokens"> <a href="#processes-and-access-tokens" title="Processes and Access Tokens">Processes and Access Tokens</a> <a href="#processes-and-access-tokens" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Processes and Access Tokens">#</a> </h2> <p>An <strong>access token</strong> describes a process or thread’s security context. It includes an account SID, group SIDs, privileges, and other security attributes. A process has a primary token, while a thread performing impersonation has an additional context to consider. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft access-token documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/access-tokens"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/access-tokens" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft access-token documentation</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Identity and permission are different questions.</strong> Knowing which account launched a program does not establish whether its current token authorizes a particular operation. Group attributes, privilege state, the requested operation, and the target object’s access-control entries all matter.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Observation</th> <th>What it establishes</th> <th>What remains unresolved</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Account belongs to Administrators</strong></td> <td>Administrative group membership</td> <td>Whether this process holds an elevated token</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Privilege appears in a token</strong></td> <td>The token contains the privilege</td> <td>Whether it is enabled and relevant to this operation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Process runs as LocalSystem</strong></td> <td>A highly privileged local identity</td> <td>Access to every remote service or protected resource</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Thread impersonates a client</strong></td> <td>A separate thread context is involved</td> <td>Which context the specific API uses</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>User Account Control (UAC)</strong> adds another distinction. In Admin Approval Mode, an administrator normally starts applications with a filtered token and elevates selected operations. An elevated process remains subject to security checks. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft explanation of UAC"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/application-security/application-control/user-account-control/how-it-works"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/application-security/application-control/user-account-control/how-it-works" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft explanation of UAC</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="supplemental-video"> <a href="#supplemental-video" title="Supplemental Video">Supplemental Video</a> <a href="#supplemental-video" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Supplemental Video">#</a> </h2> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Windows Access Tokens - From Authentication to Exploitation"> <meta itemprop="description" content="YouTube Video"> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/_ODdwpxXRR4/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_ODdwpxXRR4"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="_ODdwpxXRR4" videotitle="Windows Access Tokens - From Authentication to Exploitation" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_ODdwpxXRR4" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Windows Access Tokens - From Authentication to Exploitation"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Windows Access Tokens - From Authentication to Exploitation", "description": "YouTube Video", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/_ODdwpxXRR4\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_ODdwpxXRR4", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p><strong>Watch:</strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Windows Access Tokens - From Authentication to Exploitation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_ODdwpxXRR4"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_ODdwpxXRR4" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Windows Access Tokens - From Authentication to Exploitation</a> </span> , published by Compass Security. Use the token explanation to distinguish account identity from the privileges available to a particular process. The accompanying <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="presentations page"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.compass-security.com/en/research/presentations"> <a href="https://www.compass-security.com/en/research/presentations" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >presentations page</a> </span> provides the speaker’s material.</p> <p><strong>Viewing task:</strong> Draw a process with its primary token and a thread with an impersonation token. Explain why a username alone is insufficient evidence for predicting an access check. Compare your diagram with Microsoft’s access-token reference before moving to the lab.</p> <h2 id="inspect-your-own-context"> <a href="#inspect-your-own-context" title="Inspect Your Own Context">Inspect Your Own Context</a> <a href="#inspect-your-own-context" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Inspect Your Own Context">#</a> </h2> <p>Run these <strong>read-only commands</strong> in Command Prompt on your own Windows lab VM:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-cmd" data-lang="cmd"><span style="display:flex;"><span>whoami /user </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>whoami /groups </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>whoami /priv </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>whoami /all </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>whoami /user</code></strong> reports the account and SID. <strong><code>/groups</code></strong> shows group information, <strong><code>/priv</code></strong> shows privileges, and <strong><code>/all</code></strong> combines current-token details. Save output from the ordinary shell before opening an elevated shell for comparison. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft whoami reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/whoami"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/whoami" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft whoami reference</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> Under same-account elevation, the account SID should remain the same while token details differ. If the elevation prompt uses another account, compare the new account’s SID instead. An observed difference needs an explanation tied to the login path, not a blanket rule about administrator usernames.</p> <h2 id="read-the-registry-context"> <a href="#read-the-registry-context" title="Read the Registry Context">Read the Registry Context</a> <a href="#read-the-registry-context" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Read the Registry Context">#</a> </h2> <p>Inspect the <strong>current profile</strong> without adding or removing values:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-cmd" data-lang="cmd"><span style="display:flex;"><span>reg query <span style="color:#e6db74">"HKCU\Volatile Environment"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>reg query <span style="color:#e6db74">"HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>reg query HKU </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>reg query</code></strong> reads the named key. A missing Run key or an empty result is not an error in the exercise, since the profile might contain no startup entries there. Record the account, path, return message, and time instead of inventing an expected value. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft reg query reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/reg-query"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/reg-query" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft reg query reference</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Do not change user context mid-comparison.</strong> First relate the <strong><code>whoami</code></strong> result to the current-profile query. Then compare a second explicitly identified lab account if available. The point is to prove which identity produced the observation, not to obtain a privileged session.</p> <h2 id="hashes-responses-and-tickets"> <a href="#hashes-responses-and-tickets" title="Hashes, Responses, and Tickets">Hashes, Responses, and Tickets</a> <a href="#hashes-responses-and-tickets" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Hashes, Responses, and Tickets">#</a> </h2> <p>An <strong>NT password hash</strong> is derived from a password and is distinct from the challenge-response messages exchanged during NTLM authentication. Two identical passwords produce identical NT hashes under the same derivation. A captured NTLMv2 response is not interchangeable with the stored NT hash. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft NTLM protocol overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthn/microsoft-ntlm"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthn/microsoft-ntlm" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft NTLM protocol overview</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Pass-the-hash</strong> describes authentication using suitable password-derived material without recovering the plaintext password. Its applicability depends on the protocol, account, policy, and target service. It does not mean any hash authenticates to any application. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MITRE ATT&CK: Pass the Hash"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002/"> <a href="https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >MITRE ATT&CK: Pass the Hash</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Artifact</th> <th>Purpose</th> <th>Avoid this confusion</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>NT password hash</strong></td> <td>Password-derived secret used by relevant authentication mechanisms</td> <td>A generic file hash</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>NTLM challenge response</strong></td> <td>Proof computed for an authentication exchange</td> <td>The stored password hash</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Kerberos ticket</strong></td> <td>Credential for a ticket-based exchange</td> <td>A plaintext password</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Access token</strong></td> <td>Local security context used for authorization</td> <td>A network authentication packet</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Kerberos</strong> separates initial authentication from obtaining service tickets. Domain membership alone does not establish which protocol a particular connection used. Read the corresponding authentication evidence instead of assuming every Windows connection uses NTLM. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft Kerberos overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/kerberos/kerberos-authentication-overview"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/kerberos/kerberos-authentication-overview" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft Kerberos overview</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="place-credential-storage-correctly"> <a href="#place-credential-storage-correctly" title="Place Credential Storage Correctly">Place Credential Storage Correctly</a> <a href="#place-credential-storage-correctly" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Place Credential Storage Correctly">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Local account material</strong> belongs to the machine’s local account database, while domain account material is maintained by Active Directory. A workstation also holds authentication state and, depending on configuration, cached domain-logon information. These are different artifacts with different uses and protections. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft credential-storage explanation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/windows-authentication/credentials-processes-in-windows-authentication"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/windows-authentication/credentials-processes-in-windows-authentication" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft credential-storage explanation</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Credential availability is conditional.</strong> Privilege alone does not guarantee readable plaintext passwords or every account’s secret. Credential isolation, protected processes, sign-in method, and current session state change what exists and what an administrator is permitted to inspect. The lab needs no credential dump to demonstrate the distinction.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Question</th> <th>Appropriate evidence</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Which account is this?</strong></td> <td>Authority, account name, and SID</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Which process context applies?</strong></td> <td>Token details from the relevant process</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Which authentication occurred?</strong></td> <td>Authentication package and correlated logon records</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Which registry data was read?</strong></td> <td>Full path, loaded profile, process architecture, and timestamp</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="identity-is-more-than-ip"> <a href="#identity-is-more-than-ip" title="Identity Is More Than IP">Identity Is More Than IP</a> <a href="#identity-is-more-than-ip" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Identity Is More Than IP">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>DHCP</strong> assigns address leases and other network settings. An address often stays the same across renewals, but a later lease change is possible. An IP address is therefore an observation at a time, not a durable machine identifier.</p> <p><strong>Build a host record</strong> from hostname, account context, relevant interface addresses, and collection time. Correlate it with inventory or lease records when needed. Multiple addresses alone do not prove a host routes traffic between networks, and one address alone does not prove two observations concern the same machine.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Observation time and time zone: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Host identity and lab snapshot: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Account authority / name / SID: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Process identity and architecture: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Ordinary or elevated token: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Registry path and loaded profile: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Command and exact observed result: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Inference supported by the evidence: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Unresolved question: </span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="self-check-and-reasoning"> <a href="#self-check-and-reasoning" title="Self-Check and Reasoning">Self-Check and Reasoning</a> <a href="#self-check-and-reasoning" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Self-Check and Reasoning">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Same name, different SID:</strong> You recreate a deleted lab account named Alice. Should its old file permissions automatically follow the name?</li> <li><strong>Empty registry query:</strong> A service finds no value under its own HKCU. Has it established the user’s startup entry is absent?</li> <li><strong>Administrator without elevation:</strong> Why does a command fail even though its account belongs to Administrators?</li> <li><strong>Authentication capture:</strong> Is an NTLMv2 response the same artifact as an NT password hash?</li> <li><strong>Changed address:</strong> What additional evidence ties yesterday’s address to today’s workstation?</li> </ol> <p><strong>Expected answers:</strong> Recreated Alice is a new security principal. The service queried a different context, so it has not proved the user’s state. An administrator’s ordinary process often uses a filtered token.</p> <p><strong>Artifact and host checks:</strong> A challenge response and a stored password-derived secret serve different roles. Correlate host identity and timed inventory or DHCP evidence before joining the network observations.</p> <p><strong>Deliverable:</strong> Complete the identity record for two explicitly named lab contexts and explain one difference. Include actual command output and an interpretation. Label untested assumptions so the record remains useful when another reader repeats the exercise.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Carry the context record forward</strong> into host operations, persistence, and cleanup. A later command is easier to interpret when you already know whose token and profile it uses. Continue with <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Module 5: Command and Control Operations"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course/command-and-control-operations/"> <a href="/red-team-course/command-and-control-operations/" rel="follow me" >Module 5: Command and Control Operations</a> </span> </strong>, or return to the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="course hub"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >course hub</a> </span> </strong>.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: CompTIA A+ (220-1201): Virtualization and Cloud Computing
item.category: "CompTIA A+ Course" , "Virtualization" , "Cloud Computing" , "Hypervisors" , "IT Support" , "CompTIA Certification" , "Help Desk" , "Containers" , "VDI" , "IT Fundamentals"
item.description: Master virtualization and cloud computing for the CompTIA A+ 220-1201 Core 1 exam. Learn virtual machines, hypervisors, VDI, containers, cloud models, and cloud characteristics.
item.content:encoded: <p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Click Here to Return To the CompTIA A+ Course Page"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/a-plus-start/"> <a href="/a-plus-start/" rel="follow me" >Click Here to Return To the CompTIA A+ Course Page</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Virtualization and Cloud Computing</strong> is <strong>11%</strong> of the <strong>CompTIA A+ 220-1201 Core 1</strong> exam. This module covers virtual machines, hypervisor types, VDI, containers, cloud models, and cloud characteristics. <em>This is the smallest Core 1 domain, but the concepts appear across modern IT support.</em></p> <p>Virtualization runs many systems on one machine. Cloud computing rents that capacity from a provider so you pay only for what you use. Together they power most of the infrastructure you support today. This module gives you the vocabulary and the models.</p> <h2 id="virtualization-concepts"> <a href="#virtualization-concepts" title="Virtualization Concepts">Virtualization Concepts</a> <a href="#virtualization-concepts" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Virtualization Concepts">#</a> </h2> <p>You run software-defined computers on physical hardware.</p> <ul> <li>A <strong>virtual machine (VM)</strong> emulates a full computer with its own OS, isolated from the host.</li> <li>A <strong>sandbox</strong> restricts untrusted code and reduces host exposure. Escapes, shared folders, network access, and management mistakes remain possible.</li> <li><strong>Test and development environments</strong> let you try changes without risking production.</li> <li><strong>Snapshots</strong> capture a VM state so you roll back after a failed change.</li> </ul> <p><em>Virtualization saves money by packing many workloads onto fewer physical servers.</em></p> <h2 id="hypervisor-types"> <a href="#hypervisor-types" title="Hypervisor Types">Hypervisor Types</a> <a href="#hypervisor-types" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Hypervisor Types">#</a> </h2> <p>You pick the hypervisor that fits the workload.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Type</th> <th>Runs on</th> <th>Example</th> <th>Use</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Type 1 (bare metal)</strong></td> <td>Directly on hardware</td> <td>ESXi, Hyper-V, Proxmox VE</td> <td>Data centers, servers</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Type 2 (hosted)</strong></td> <td>On top of an OS</td> <td>VirtualBox, VMware Workstation</td> <td>Desktops, labs, testing</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Type 1</strong> hypervisors run directly on host hardware, while <strong>Type 2</strong> products run through a host OS. Security and speed depend on the product, workload, patch level, and configuration. Neither type guarantees guest isolation.</p> <h2 id="virtualization-requirements"> <a href="#virtualization-requirements" title="Virtualization Requirements">Virtualization Requirements</a> <a href="#virtualization-requirements" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Virtualization Requirements">#</a> </h2> <p>You meet the prerequisites before a VM runs well.</p> <ul> <li><strong>CPU support</strong> for <strong>Intel VT-x</strong> or <strong>AMD-V</strong>, enabled in UEFI.</li> <li>Enough <strong>RAM</strong> to allocate to each guest plus the host.</li> <li><strong>Storage</strong> for virtual disks, ideally on fast SSDs.</li> <li><strong>Network</strong> configuration with bridged, NAT, or host-only adapters.</li> <li><strong>Security</strong> isolation controls to reduce guest-to-host risk. Account for VM escapes, shared resources, network paths, and management mistakes.</li> </ul> <h2 id="desktop-virtualization-and-containers"> <a href="#desktop-virtualization-and-containers" title="Desktop Virtualization and Containers">Desktop Virtualization and Containers</a> <a href="#desktop-virtualization-and-containers" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Desktop Virtualization and Containers">#</a> </h2> <p>You deliver desktops and apps without local installs.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI)</strong> hosts user desktops on a central server, streamed to thin clients.</li> <li><strong>Containers</strong> package an app with its dependencies but share the host OS kernel, so they are lighter than VMs.</li> </ul> <p>Containers start in seconds and use less memory than full VMs. To understand the trade-offs, read <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker vs VMs"> <meta
